---
title: "Agent-based Models for Multi-analyst Studies"
---
**Presenter:** Dominik Dianovics, Eötvös Loránd University

**Co-authors:** Alexandra Sarafoglou (University of Amsterdam), Aljoscha Rimpler (University of Groningen), Don van Ravenzwaaij (University of Groningen), Noah Van Dongen (Erasmus University)

### Abstract {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A many-analysts study refers to a research design in which multiple independent analysts, teams, or laboratories analyze the same data and investigate the same research question while maintaining their own analytical decisions, workflows, and theoretical assumptions (Aczel et al., 2021). This design serves to quantify analytical variability to assess the robustness of results obtained along heterogeneous decision paths, and to explore how researchers' freedom and diverse perspectives shape scientific conclusions.

Several issues remain unclear regarding multi-analyst studies. There are several methods for aggregating estimates, such as simple median, weighted averaging, or estimation similar to meta-analysis. In addition, it is necessary to examine the research questions analysts answer, as the accuracy of quantitative estimates may be influenced by the difficulty of the question, the magnitude of the hypothesized effect, and the strength and direction of the evidence.

To assess the accuracy of researchers' estimates, it is necessary to know the ground truth, which refers to the actual effect behind the research question. We compare this with the researchers' estimates. To obtain this ground truth, data simulation can be used. To avoid the bias that arises when researchers coincidentally use the same method we use to simulate the data — leading to overly precise estimates — we employ an agent-based model for data generation. This method allows us to define pre-determined probabilities that influence data generation through the interactions of agents and their environment at each step of the simulation. The more complex the behavior we are modeling, the harder it is to model these interactions, since the model is not deterministic but probabilistic.

By presenting our proposed study and its underlying model, we intend to show its usefulness for studies requiring simulation, for assessing methodologies for improving the accuracy of estimates, and for studying the statistical wisdom of crowds under a many-analysts design.
